entries.title: Therese Boyle wins Far Southwest Side District 9b in Chicago School Board race
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/school-board/districts/9b/" target="_blank" ><i><u>District 9b</u></i></a><i> neighborhoods: Roseland, West Pullman, Morgan Park, Beverly, Mount Greenwood, Washington Heights </i></p><p>Incumbent <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/therese-boyle/" target="_blank" ><u>Therese Boyle</u></a>, a retired Chicago Public Schools psychologist, was re-elected to represent the Far Southwest Side on the Chicago School Board.</p><p>She easily defeated her Chicago Teachers Union-backed challenger <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/katherine-s-dunneback/" target="_blank" ><u>Katherine Dunneback</u></a>. Boyle won nearly 73% of the vote with 87% of the precincts counted, according to results from the Associated Press early Wednesday morning.</p><p>Boyle was first elected two years ago and was endorsed by groups that oppose the powerful Chicago Teachers Union.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/therese-boyle/" target="_blank" ><u>Boyle</u></a> spent 35 years working for the district, while <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/katherine-s-dunneback/" target="_blank" ><u>Dunneback</u></a> is a former CPS mom and speech-language pathologist currently working as an adjunct clinical professor at Saint Xavier University. They competed to represent an area with 46 public schools, most of which are neighborhood schools, with few privately run charters and lottery-based magnets.</p><p>Boyle was <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/chicago-school-board/2026/09/21/key-education-endorsements-for-cps-school-board-candidates" target="_blank" ><u>endorsed</u></a> by groups that oppose the teachers union and support school choice, and she was also backed by the Service Employees International Union, which represents thousands of CPS support staff and has split politically with the teachers union in recent years. Dunneback was endorsed by the Chicago Teachers Union.</p><p>Boyle credits her longtime roots in tight-knit Mount Greenwood, where she’s lived for nearly 40 years, for helping her win over voters.</p><p>“The people who talked to the voters were my friends and family and neighbors and fellow colleagues,” Boyle said. “I think that helped.”</p><p>Having the support of SEIU, whose members helped knock on doors, helped, too, Boyle said.</p><p>Dunneback had not called to concede, Boyle said Tuesday night. Dunneback could not immediately be reached for comment.</p><p>Enrollment is an issue across much of the district, with just 13% of CPS students choosing to attend their zoned public high schools, according to <a class="Link" href="https://projects.chalkbeat.org/2026/chicago-school-board-election-map/?loader=true&initialWidth=690&windowHeight=501&parentTitle=Chicago%2520school%2520board%2520election%25202026%2520voter%2520guide%253A%2520District%252010a%2520candidates%2520-%2520Chalkbeat&parentUrl=https%253A%252F%252Fwww.chalkbeat.org%252Fchicago%252F2026%252F09%252F24%252Fschool-board-election-2026-district-10a-candidates-voter-guide%252F" target="_blank" ><u>data compiled by Chalkbeat</u></a>. Nearly 57% chose their local elementary school. The majority of students in this school board district are Black, while 10% are Hispanic and 11% are white. The majority of schools in the area were designated last year as “commendable,” the state’s second highest ranking.</p><p>Both Dunneback and Boyle had children attend Chicago Public Schools for a time before going to private schools. Boyle said one of her daughters attended a Beverly public school for preschool. Dunneback’s children attended a Morgan Park neighborhood elementary school.</p><p>Boyle said residents are focused on making sure the district is “spending money wisely,” while Dunneback said her neighbors are concerned about school overcrowding and closures.</p><p>The two candidates agreed on academics, including imposing strict limits on AI and electronic devices, but disagreed on charter schools and school closures. Boyle favors charter schools and school consolidation when equitable and cost effective. Dunneback opposes charter schools and spoke of expanding a CPS and CTU program that turns neighborhood schools into community hubs as an alternative to closures.</p><p>Neither candidate wants to<a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/chicago-school-board/2026/10/13/long-a-foregone-conclusion-property-tax-hikes-will-no-longer-be-a-given-under-elected-cps-board" target="_blank" ><u> raise property taxes to the maximum to fund schools</u></a>, according to our CPS School Board questionnaire. But Boyle says CPS is not spending wisely, whereas Dunneback says board members should work with other elected officials to fund schools through other tax policies.</p><p>Boyle <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-campaign-finance/" target="_blank" ><u>received contributions</u></a> from the SEIU IL Council political action committee and the Common Ground Collective, a PAC that is anti-CTU and heavily funded by billionaire Michael Sacks. Dunneback’s top contributions were from the CTU-affiliated Our Schools PAC and CTU PAC.</p><p><i>Contributing: Jim Lynch of Block Club Chicago</i><br></p>

entries.title: Downtown and Near North Side District 6a Chicago School Board race too close to call
entries.summary:
District 6a neighborhoods: Near North Side, West Town

The candidate supported by a billionaire-backed political group and charter proponents had a narrow lead over two progressives as of early Wednesday, but the race was too close to call.

With all precincts reporting, less than 1,000 votes separated Isaiah White, a school support worker; Anusha Thotakura, the incumbent who runs a statewide advocacy organization; and Brenda Lee Anderson, a Northwestern University lecturer on leave, according to the Associated Press.

The close race was somewhat unexpected. Voters in the area typically support more conservative candidates. But across the city, candidates supported by the Chicago Teachers Union are doing better than expected after being significantly outspent.

Thotakura got support from the CTU and the Service Employees International Union, which represents school support workers. She seems to be splitting the more left-leaning vote with Anderson, who was not backed by any special interests.

More than $500,000 was spent on White’s campaign by The Urban Center, a centrist political organization that advocates for school choice across public and private schools, and the political arm of the Illinois Network of Charter Schools. He also was endorsed by an anti-CTU political action committee that is heavily funded by billionaire Michael Sacks and says it aims to engage voters around “effective progressive policies.”

Given its location as part of the commercial and business center of the city, District 6a has just 14 public schools — the fewest of any school board electoral districts — and none are neighborhood high schools. The students who attend Chicago Public Schools here include a more diverse mix than in most districts, but the schools have more white and Asian American students than CPS as a whole.

Two of the schools in the district have the highest rating given by the state; while 60% had the lowest two distinctions, “developing” and “comprehensive,” according to 2026 state data released last week. There are now six levels of designations, up from the five up last year when the bottom two were called “comprehensive” and “intensive.”

Thotakura’s and White’s main priorities are to boost reading and math scores. Anderson’s main goal is to fix CPS’ chronic budget crisis.

Contributing: Reema Amin, Chalkbeat Chicago
entries.author: Sarah Karp

entries.title: Carlos Rivas Jr. trails slightly behind Jason Dónes in District 3b Chicago School Board race
entries.summary:
District 3b neighborhoods: Humboldt Park, Logan Square, Belmont Cragin, West Town, Hermosa

Incumbent Carlos Rivas Jr. and Jason Dónes were neck and neck early Wednesday morning Tuesday night in their contest for a school board seat representing a district on the Near Northwest Side, according to Associated Press election results.

Bolstered by about $600,000 from groups that oppose the Chicago Teachers Union, Rivas, a former-teacher-turned city communications director, trailed ever so slightly behind Jason Dónes, with about five of 74 precincts still to be counted.

It was a rematch for two men who both grew up in Humboldt Park, graduated from selective-enrollment Chicago public high schools, and became teachers through Teach for America. In 2024 Rivas Jr. won with 54% of the vote.

Both candidates identify as progressives. Rivas has taken a more fiscally conservative approach to the school budget than his opponent.

He had support from the Service Employees International Union, which represents thousands of CPS school support staff and has split politically with the teachers union in recent years. Also behind him were charter school advocates, some Northwest Side officials and the the Common Ground Collective, a political action committee that opposes the CTU, is heavily funded by billionaire Michael Sacks and says it aims to engage voters around “effective progressive policies.”

Jason Dónes was backed by the CTU and several Northwest Side elected officials.

A few days before the election, Rivas responded to the release of records that showed he was suspended from his job at a charter school in 2018 after he became intoxicated at a work event and engaged in “unwanted touching” of a co-worker.

Rivas said the incident happened at a difficult time in his life when he was caring for his dying mother and that he took responsibility for what happened and got help through an employee assistance program.

“I believe in accountability, growth and second chances,” he told the Chicago Sun-Times in a statement. Rivas worked as a teacher, college counselor and external affairs manager at the school. He is now the public affairs director for the Civilian Office of Police Accountability.

Schools in District 3b are struggling with teacher and counselor shortages, higher property taxes, and low enrollment amid rapid gentrification. The district includes a mix of 32 schools serving mostly Latino students. The schools are generally strong, with about 60% achieving the state’s second highest rating last year. But 6% have the lowest of the five ratings.

Rivas and Dónes both care about protecting immigrant students from federal immigration agents, supporting more affordable housing, and securing more resources and community partnerships for CPS families. Rivas says he wants less interference from the mayor on the board and to move away from using loans that will increase CPS’ budget deficit.

Dónes, a CPS parent, was looking to increase budget transparency, push for creative solutions within the existing budget framework, and said on our questionnaire that he wouldn’t accept contributions from corporations or “private interest groups funded by billionaires and millionaires.”

Rivas’ outside support was about five times greater than Dónes’. As of Monday, more than half of the $502,000 backing Rivas came from the political arm of the Illinois Network of Charter Schools while another $123,000 came from the anti-CTU Common Ground Collective. All of Dónes’ outside support comes from the CTU, totaling about $22,000.

Contributing: Ariel Parrella-Aureli, Block Club Chicago
entries.author: Lauren FitzPatrick

entries.title: Claudia Peralta wins Far Northwest Side District 1b Chicago School Board race
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://graphics-stage.suntimes.com/esb/school-board/districts/1b/" target="_blank" ><i><u>District 1b</u></i></a><i> neighborhoods: Portage Park, Dunning, Irving Park, Belmont Cragin, North Park, Montclare, Albany Park</i></p><p><a class="Link" href="https://graphics-stage.suntimes.com/esb/candidates/claudia-peralta/" target="_blank" ><u>Claudia Peralta</u></a>, a longtime political aide and Chicago Public Schools parent, won her first bid for office representing the Far North Side on Chicago’s fully elected school board, with her opponent saying Tuesday night she’ll call her with congratulations in the morning.</p><p>In one of the city’s most expensive races, Peralta defeated education consultant <a class="Link" href="https://graphics-stage.suntimes.com/esb/candidates/michelle-n-pierre/" target="_blank" ><u>Michelle Pierre</u>, winning nearly 63% of the votes with all precincts reporting</a>, according to Associated Press election results. That’s despite groups who support school choice and sought to fend off the Chicago Teachers Union spending more than $800,000 to defeat her.</p><p>“I'm really excited,” Peralta said by telephone.</p><p>She said she knocked on thousands of doors to talk with voters, a philosophy she plans to bring to the school board in January.</p><p>“People power works,” she said. “We beat dark money today. Chicagoans on the Far Northwest Side should feel really proud of that.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://graphics-stage.suntimes.com/esb/candidates/claudia-peralta/" target="_blank" ><u>Peralta</u></a> was making her debut as a candidate, but has worked with multiple politicians on the Northwest Side, including her current role as district director for U.S. Rep. Delia Ramirez. <a class="Link" href="https://graphics-stage.suntimes.com/esb/candidates/michelle-n-pierre/" target="_blank" ><u>Pierre</u></a> lost by a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/chicago-school-board/2024/11/05/election-results-district-1-far-northwest-side-pierre-custer" target="_blank" ><u>thin margin in 2024</u></a>, which was her first time running for office after spending more than 25 years working in education as a teacher, principal in public and charter schools, district administrator and leadership coach.</p><p>This matchup wasn’t so much about individual policies as it was about differing strategies for how to govern as a Chicago School Board member.</p><p>An educator for decades, Pierre is metrics-driven, weighing district financial decisions against their return on investment for students bettering their academic outcomes. Peralta is rooted in political savvy and using government relationships to secure the resources Chicago Public Schools needs for students to thrive.</p><p>Outside groups spent heavily on this race. As of Monday, it had attracted more spending by political action committees and super PACs — more than $830,000 — than any other school board district.</p><p>More than half of that came from the anti-CTU Common Ground Collective, and has thrown money behind Pierre and against Peralta, who was endorsed by the CTU. Pierre also got funding from the political arm of the Illinois Network of Charter Schools and The Urban Center, an organization that advocates for centrist leadership and school choice, including private schools.</p><p>Instead Pierre said that money and the public’s perception about billionaires interfering in elections ended up hurting her chances.</p><p>“I definitely feel like a misrepresentation of what I stood for, of pushing a narrative around the billionaires was very hard on my community,” Pierre said. “That definitely did not represent me or what I believe or what I would do on the board, but that narrative was shared constantly and so, that is where we're at.”</p><p>“I applaud Claudia for running a really good race and can't wait to see what she does on the board. But I'm really proud of the race that I ran and the belief system I believe that every child should have a great education from K-12, and that we should be fiscally sound for our community. That's what I will always advocate for and that's what I've done.</p><p>“The people have spoken about what kind of leadership they want on the school board,” Pierre said, “and Claudia is that person.”</p><p>The winner will replace Jennifer Custer, who has served the past two years and ran for school board president before <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-school-board/2026/08/27/jennifer-custer-drops-out-of-race-for-chicago-school-board-president" target="_blank" ><u>dropping out of the race in August</u></a>.</p><p>District 1b is home to 20 Chicago public schools, which is among the fewest of all the school board voting districts. Families here choose their neighborhood elementary schools at a higher rate than in other parts of the city — but not their high schools. Students who attend school in this district are mostly Hispanic — 69% — while 19% are white and 5% are Black, according to <a class="Link" href="https://projects.chalkbeat.org/2026/chicago-school-board-election-map/?loader=true&initialWidth=690&windowHeight=501&parentTitle=Chicago%2520school%2520board%2520election%25202026%2520voter%2520guide%253A%2520District%252010a%2520candidates%2520-%2520Chalkbeat&parentUrl=https%253A%252F%252Fwww.chalkbeat.org%252Fchicago%252F2026%252F09%252F24%252Fschool-board-election-2026-district-10a-candidates-voter-guide%252F#districtNumber=1b" target="_blank" ><u>data compiled by Chalkbeat</u></a>.</p><p><i>Contributing: Makiya Seminera, Chalkbeat Chicago</i></p>
entries.author: Lauren FitzPatrick

entries.title: Lozano leads in District 7a Chicago School Board race
entries.summary:
District 7a neighborhoods: South Lawndale, Near West Side, Lower West Side, Garfield Ridge, Archer Heights

Longtime Pilsen activist Emma Lozano was leading in this majority-Latino district as of early Wednesday but the race was too close to call.

Lozano had received 54% of the vote with 82% of precincts reporting, according to the Associated Press.

Lozano, first appointed in 2024 by Mayor Brandon Johnson, faced a challenge from Jesus Ayala Jr., a Chicago Public Schools graduate who worked for a nonprofit after-school program.

Lozano was endorsed by the Chicago Teachers Union, while Ayala had the backing of charter school advocates, groups that oppose the CTU and the Service Employees International Union Illinois State Council — which represents thousands of support staff in CPS and has split politically with the teachers union in recent years. Ayala tried to run in 2024, but his name was removed from the ballot after a successful challenge to the signatures on his nomination paperwork.

Ayala had raised $74,000 more than Lozano but she said the decades she spent advocating for education issues gave her the edge in the race.

“I think people remember that and that was able to carry me through,” Lozano said just after 10 p.m.

For Lozano, being part of Tuesday’s election felt like a revolutionary act, recalling a time when community members fought to get an elected school board. She was critical of how much money was poured into the various races.

Lozano will have to work with Jessica Biggs, who won the race for board president and was supported by groups who oppose the Chicago Teachers Union. Lozano said she would respect the election results but she won’t budge on her principles when it comes time to vote on matters before the board.

“There’s going to be some times, hopefully not just myself but others, will have to keep [Biggs] in her place,” Lozano said, adding that she wants to ensure resources are allocated to students living in mixed-status immigrant homes and providing better school lunches.

This Southwest Side district is home to 48 public schools. Last year, 64% received the state’s second-highest designation, “commendable,” while 4.5% received an “intensive” designation, indicating they remained among the bottom 5% of low-income schools in the state for four years after receiving comprehensive support or continued to have a graduation rate of 67% or below.

The students who attend District 7a schools are primarily Latino, matching the community demographics, and most come from families with low incomes. Nearly half are English learners.

Both Lozano and Ayala identified protecting immigrant communities and securing progressive revenue among their priorities.

entries.title: Debby Pope wins in North Side District 2b Chicago School Board race
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/school-board/districts/2b/" target="_blank" ><i><u>District 2b</u></i></a><i> neighborhoods: Lincoln Square, Edgewater, Albany Park, Uptown, North Park </i></p><p>Debby Pope, a retired teacher backed by the Chicago Teachers Union, prevailed in the school board’s closely watched District 2b race, retaining the seat she was appointed to by Mayor Brandon Johnson.</p><p>Pope easily defeated former special education teacher Kyna Lenhof, who was backed by groups critical of the CTU. As of early Wednesday, Pope had 63% of the vote with nearly 96% of precincts reporting, according to the Associated Press.</p><p>Pope attributed her win to her “decades of experience” as a teacher, parent and community member who has lived in her district for many years.</p><p>“I think that it’s my years of work that have paid off,” Pope said.</p><p>She said backing from the CTU also helped her, but noted that it wasn’t “anything like” the support that Lenhof received from political groups like the Common Ground Collective.</p><p>“It shows that the school board cannot be bought so easily,” Pope said.</p><p>District 2b is one of Chicago’s most culturally diverse areas and is home to 18 public schools. Students who attend schools in the district are 40% Hispanic, 30% white, nearly 15% Asian American and 9% Black, <a class="Link" href="https://projects.chalkbeat.org/2026/chicago-school-board-election-map/?loader=true&initialWidth=690&windowHeight=501&parentTitle=Chicago%2520school%2520board%2520election%25202026%2520voter%2520guide%253A%2520District%252010a%2520candidates%2520-%2520Chalkbeat&parentUrl=https%253A%252F%252Fwww.chalkbeat.org%252Fchicago%252F2026%252F09%252F24%252Fschool-board-election-2026-district-10a-candidates-voter-guide%252F#districtNumber=2b" target="_blank" ><u>according to data compiled by Chalkbeat</u></a>.</p><p>Though none of the schools in the district last year earned the state’s highest rating of “exemplary,” a high share, 79%, earned the state’s second-highest rating of “commendable,” <a class="Link" href="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/SVkXB/1/index.html" target="_blank" ><u>data compiled by Chalkbeat shows</u></a>.</p><p>And 62% of students in District 2b chose to attend their neighborhood school — the second-highest share in the city and well above CPS average of 46%.</p><p>Both candidates touted their experience working in classrooms and listed adequate classroom funding and resources among their main priorities. But their thoughts on how to secure that varied.</p><p>Pope said she supports increasing funding for schools by taxing the rich, while Lenhof said she wants to reduce the district’s reliance on high-interest loans.</p><p>Johnson appointed Pope to the board 2024 after the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2024/10/04/all-cps-board-members-to-resign-adding-to-school-district-chaos" target="_blank" ><u>mass resignation of his first group</u></a> of school board appointees amid tensions with former CPS CEO Pedro Martinez.</p><p>She got the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/07/13/ctu-endorses-15-school-board-candidates-throwing-weight-behind-incumbents-mayoral-picks" target="_blank" ><u>nod from the powerful teachers union</u></a>, while Lenhof was endorsed by<a class="Link" href="https://theurbancenter.org/what-we-stand-for/#access-to-quality-schools" target="_blank" ><u> The Urban Center</u></a><a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/p/DcLn64Ikau1/?img_index=4" target="_blank" ><u>,</u></a> a centrist political organization that supports charters and advocates for school choice across public and private schools. Lenhof was also endorsed by <a class="Link" href="https://cgcollective.org/endorsements" target="_blank" ><u>the Common Ground Collective</u></a>, which is heavily funded by billionaire Michael Sacks and says it aims to engage voters around “effective progressive policies.”</p><p>Lenhof’s campaign was <a class="Link" href="https://graphics-stage.suntimes.com/chicago-school-board-campaign-finance/" target="_blank" ><u>buoyed by contributions</u></a> from Common Ground and the political arm of the Illinois Network of Charter Schools, while much of Pope’s support came from the CTU and groups aligned with the union, including the Chicago Working Families PAC.</p><p>Earlier this summer, Common Ground <a class="Link" href="https://www.facebook.com/commongroundcoll/videos/1052224493829440/" target="_blank" ><u>released an ad</u></a> attacking Pope for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-school-board/2026/07/30/chicago-school-board-approves-budget-that-reverses-layoffs-but-counts-on-shaky-state-funds" target="_blank" ><u>voting in favor of a CPS budget plan</u></a> that assumed the district would receive $150 million more in state funding than projected. The day before the vote, Lenhof also <a class="Link" href="https://kynaforthekids.org/" target="_blank" ><u>released a statement criticizing Pope</u></a>.</p><p><i>Contributing: Molly DeVore, Block Club Chicago</i></p>

entries.title: West Side District 5b Chicago School Board race too close to call
entries.summary:
District 5b neighborhoods: North Lawndale, Near West Side, East Garfield Park, West Garfield Park, West Town 

Michilla “Kyla” Blaise was leading in District 5b early Wednesday morning, but the school board race was too close to declare a winner.

Blaise led with nearly 53% of the votes with about 95% of precincts reporting, according to the Associated Press.

Blaise, a political aide backed by the Chicago Teachers Union, was appointed by Mayor Brandon Johnson to the school board in 2024, and she was seeking a two-year seat on the school board representing a large swath of the West Side.

For challenger Anthony Hargrove, it was his second attempt at the seat after failing to make the ballot two years ago. Hargrove, who runs programs to help dropouts get back in school, had support from the Service Employees International Union Illinois State Council, which represents CPS support staff, charter school advocates like the Illinois Network of Charter Schools and the Common Ground Collective, an anti-CTU political action committee that’s heavily funded by billionaire Michael Sacks.

Blaise and Hargrove had not responded to a request for comment as of early Wednesday.

District 5b is one of the school board’s most economically diverse, stretching from the wealthy West Loop to historically disinvested neighborhoods such as North Lawndale and Garfield Park. It includes several neighborhood high schools struggling with declining enrollment, as well as some of CPS’ most in-demand magnet schools. Students who attend school here are mostly Black and Hispanic.

Students in District 5b are less likely to attend their neighborhood school than students in any other voting district in the city. Only 6% chose their local high school, while 35% chose their neighborhood elementary school.

The candidates homed in on different issues during the race. Blaise said she was focused on increasing funding for CPS, addressing declining enrollment and improving student mental health, while Hargrove zeroed in on improving reading and math proficiency, refining special education and expanding vocational and career education.

The two candidates aligned on some issues. They both support stronger restrictions on the use of artificial intelligence and cellphones in the classroom, and both oppose closing schools for any reason.

Notably, Blaise led the effort to pass a CPS budget that reversed some proposed cuts but banked on the state to provide $150 million in funding it had not committed. On his candidate questionnaire, Hargrove said the school board should continue to advocate for additional state funding and look for other savings “before cutting classroom programs or student services.”

Contributing: Mary Norkol

entries.title: Yesenia Lopez retains District 7b seat in Chicago School Board election
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/school-board/districts/7b/" target="_blank" ><i><u>District 7b</u></i></a><i> neighborhoods: Brighton Park, Lower West Side, Archer Heights, Bridgeport, Gage Park, West Elsdon, Armour Square, McKinley Park</i></p><p>Despite losing the backing of the Chicago Teachers Union, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/yesenia-lopez/" target="_blank" ><u>Yesenia Lopez</u></a> was elected Tuesday to serve four more years on the school board.</p><p>As of early Wednesday morning she received 69% of the vote with 97% of precincts reporting, according to the Associated Press.</p><p>Lopez fended off a challenge from <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/erika-e-diaz-chavez/" target="_blank" ><u>Erika Diaz-Chavez</u></a>, a project manager at the Chicago Park District, who attended private schools growing up. Diaz-Chavez’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-campaign-finance/" target="_blank" ><u>biggest campaign donation</u></a> came from the Illinois Network of Charter Schools’ political arm. The Urban Center, which promotes school choice and private schools, also contributed to her campaign.</p><p>In a statement, Diaz-Chavez said the results were not what she hoped for but she remained grateful to those who supported her campaign.</p><p>“I am proud of the campaign we ran and the people who stood alongside me,” Diaz-Chavez said. “My commitment to our children, families, and community has not changed.”</p><p>Lopez, who will represent a slice of the Southwest Side, was first elected to the board in 2024. This time around, she was backed by the Service Employees International Union Illinois State Council, which represents thousands of CPS support staff and has split politically with the teachers union in recent years. She was also endorsed by <a class="Link" href="https://publicschoolchampions.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Our Schools Chicago</u></a>. That group’s views are aligned with the CTU and <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/chicago-school-board/2026/09/21/key-education-endorsements-for-cps-school-board-candidates" target="_blank" ><u>endorsed</u></a> all the same candidates plus Lopez.</p><p>There are 34 schools in District 7b, 13% of which ranked among the top 10% in Illinois last year. A majority of the schools — 73% — received the second-highest designation, “commendable,” and 13% of the schools were designated as “targeted,” meaning that one or more student groups are at or below the level of all students in the lowest-performing 5% of schools.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://projects.chalkbeat.org/2026/chicago-school-board-election-map/?loader=true&initialWidth=690&windowHeight=501&parentTitle=Chicago%2520school%2520board%2520election%25202026%2520voter%2520guide%253A%2520District%252010a%2520candidates%2520-%2520Chalkbeat&parentUrl=https%253A%252F%252Fwww.chalkbeat.org%252Fchicago%252F2026%252F09%252F24%252Fschool-board-election-2026-district-10a-candidates-voter-guide%252F#districtNumber=7b" target="_blank" ><u>District 7b schools</u></a> serve the highest percentage of Hispanic students in CPS, but a few schools also serve predominantly Asian American students. About 84% of students come from families with low incomes, and around half are English learners.</p><p>Both candidates said they wanted to provide more special education resources for students in response to parents’ concerns. They also want to ensure CPS is doing enough to protect immigrant families amid increased immigration enforcement in the city.</p><p>But their views diverged on Sustainable Community Schools, a program favored by the CTU that gives dozens of schools additional funds to partner with community organizations and provide extra services for families.</p><p>Diaz-Chavez isn’t sure the model is delivering results and wants to evaluate the program before spending more money on it. Lopez sees the model as a boon to families and supports it, though she agrees the district should track its progress.</p>

entries.title: Connie Anderson holds on to District 10b seat in Chicago School Board race
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/school-board/districts/10b/" target="_blank" ><i><u>District 10b</u></i></a><i> neighborhoods: South Deering, Hegewisch, Riverdale, East Side, Chatham, South Chicago, Pullman, Calumet Heights, Avalon Park, Burnside, South Shore </i></p><p>A mom who ran for school board to fight for more funding for special needs students like her daughter has won her bid to represent District 10b on the city’s Southeast Side.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/connie-anderson/" target="_blank" ><u>Connie Anderson</u></a>, the incumbent backed by the Chicago Teachers Union, triumphed over Patrick Watson, the lead legislative aide for 9th Ward Ald. Anthony Beale, one of Mayor Brandon Johnson’s fiercest critics.</p><p>Anderson had nearly 63% of the vote with 92% of precincts reporting as of early Wednesday morning, according to the Associated Press.</p><p>Watson received more than $300,000 in support from pro-charter school groups, as well as the Common Ground Collective, an anti-CTU political group that’s largely funded by billionaire Michael Sacks. Meanwhile, Anderson had only $60,000 in her campaign coffers.</p><p>Anderson said she questioned whether she could pull off a win when she realized how much she was being outspent.</p><p>“Then, lo and behold, you're looking at the polls, and you're like, ‘Wait, what?’” she said. “People believe in my platform, they believe in me, and it's just so surreal.”</p><p>Anderson said she’s happy that she’ll remain on the board with a group of other CTU-supported candidates and she’s ready to get to work.</p><p>“It means we're going to have some real discussions on how we're going to manage this budget and how we're going to get out of the red,” she said. “It means that we're not going to continue to line the pockets of people that are not benefiting our kids.”</p><p>Also defeated was write-in candidate <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/rosita-chatonda/" target="_blank" ><u>Rosita Chatonda</u></a>, a former teacher who spent years challenging her CPS firing that landed her on the district’s “do not hire” list. Chatonda had no donations on file.</p><p>Anderson, a paralegal and mom of twins who attend CPS, got a leg up when Johnson appointed her to fill the vacant seat in July after she filed her paperwork to run in June.</p><p>With 58 schools and 21,844 students enrolled, this school board electoral district has the second-most public schools and students. Two-thirds of its students are Black and 31% are Latino.</p><p>Only 7% of the schools in the area are considered exemplary — the state’s highest rating — and 29% received the lowest designation, which is comprehensive, according to 2026 data.</p><p>Watson had charged that Anderson’s recent appointment was “indicative of the games being played.” She got the endorsement of the CTU, which is closely aligned with the mayor.</p><p>“I just don't think politics belongs in education,” Watson said. “I think education belongs in education.”</p><p>The three candidates disagreed on the Illinois Quantum & Microelectronics Park, the massive research and technology facility being built in their district. Anderson doubted it would have a positive impact on schools, citing pushback over a contractual agreement.</p><p>But Chatonda saw possibilities and Watson said it was “an excellent opportunity for CPS.”</p>

entries.title: Addressing, adapting to Chicago's water system needs
entries.summary: <p>In the last decade, I have led the Chicago Department of Water Management twice. When I returned in 2024 after leaving in 2020, I saw how much the work of this urban water utility had changed.</p><p>Our mission remains the same: providing safe, high-quality drinking water and maintaining the infrastructure Chicagoans depend on. But our city’s challenges have changed, and our work must change with them.</p><p>Today, we face more intense rainfall, localized flooding, aging infrastructure and a historic effort to remove <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/06/30/chicago-has-most-lead-pipes-why-is-it-so-expensive-to-replace-them" >lead service lines</a>. Meeting these challenges requires rethinking what a modern water utility must do.</p><p>This summer’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/01/chicago-rain-flooding-lollapalooza" >extraordinary rainfall</a> exposed the limitations of infrastructure built over generations in an increasingly developed city. When heavy rain overwhelms sewers, the consequences include flooded streets, basement backups and property damage.</p><p>That is why the Department of Water Management is exploring new approaches to stormwater management. Through a partnership with the Metropolitan Water Reclamation District of Greater Chicago, we are piloting underground “wing” storage on the West Side. Together, the projects will provide nearly 1.7 million gallons of additional stormwater storage, temporarily holding runoff to give local sewers more capacity.</p><p>Innovation means expanding our toolbox, applying engineering principles in new ways and partnering with other agencies to solve problems more effectively.</p><p>The same thinking applies to lead service line replacement. Removing these lines is a critical public health priority and one of Chicago’s largest infrastructure efforts. It also changes how we plan construction, maintain infrastructure, train workers and allocate resources.</p><p>We cannot choose between maintaining our system and replacing lead lines. We must do both with limited additional funding. By leveraging available funding and incorporating replacements into capital improvement projects, we can advance this work more efficiently and equitably.</p><p>Flooding and lead replacement are different challenges, but they share a lesson: a water utility cannot stand still.</p><p>We must maintain the system Chicago inherited while building the system Chicago needs. That requires strong partnerships, workforce investment and a willingness to test new approaches.</p><p>Above all, it requires Department of Water Management employees who turn plans into progress in neighborhoods across Chicago. Our responsibility is not simply to maintain the water system we inherited, but to improve the system we pass on to the next generation.</p><p><i>Randy Conner, commissioner, Chicago Department of Water Management</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-3f0000" name="module-3f0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Don’t destroy iconic Chicago monument</h3><h3></h3><p>On a recent a trip to Paris, I commented to my husband, “I had forgotten how incredibly beautiful this city is. The architecture is gorgeous ... one building after the next after the next. Block after block after block. I so appreciate the beauty and grandeur of Paris architecture. I wish Chicago had more buildings like this.” </p><p>So it got me thinking why it's critically important to preserve what we do have.</p><p>Chicago is renowned for its beautiful and diverse architecture. It's our responsibility to protect and preserve it, as well as to ensure that it's presented in all its glory. So, I can't even begin to understand why anyone would consider, fund and approve of a project to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2026/09/21/griffin-museum-science-industry-design-ramsa-drawing-board" >transform </a>the north entrance of the Griffin Museum of Science and Industry. Developing a structure that blocks the visual of this beautiful, historic and classical-style work of art is heinous enough. But actually upsetting the construction of the monument itself (yes, I do consider it a monument) is almost criminal.</p><p>Given the museum's historic value, being housed in the remaining structure of the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition, as well as one of the few examples of Classical Revival architecture, we should be doing everything in our power to conserve and safeguard this unique and special asset. In light of the other structural changes occurring at the Griffin MSI — specifically at the south portico — this change seems wholly unnecessary while it simultaneously <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/letters-to-the-editor/2026/09/23/griffin-museum-of-science-and-industry-cta-artificial-intelligence-ai" >disrespects</a> the genius and artistry of Charles B. Atwood and D. H. Burnham & Company.</p><p>Please leave the north portico entrance of the museum as is. This incredible piece of art deserves to be viewed without obstruction, so all can appreciate the beauty and grandeur it brings to our wonderful city.</p><p><i>Annie McEnroe, Lincoln Park</i></p><h3>Chicago media treated Angel Reese fairly </h3><p>Sun-Times columnist Scoop Jackson’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/10/30/sky-did-angel-reese-a-favor-by-dealing-her-to-dream" >analysis</a> of Angel Reese is accurate in that it highlights how she has matured and blossomed since leaving the Sky. However, his accusation that the local media, “unused to seeing an overt-spoken leader of one of our professional teams, weren’t prepared for an overt, cultured superstar athlete” is not accurate. </p><p>Chicago has had numerous “overt, cultured superstars” that the media have followed and evaluated with candor and objectivity (does the name Michael Jordan ring a bell?)</p><p>Yes, Reese is a great player, and yes, Atlanta is a good fit, but don’t blame Chicago media for the chip on Angel’s shoulder.</p><p><i>Sheryl Gallaher, Palos Park</i></p><h3>Dope pope</h3><p>If anyone has any doubts that our current pope is a true Chicagoan, they need only to be reminded that he <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/pope-leo-xiv/2026/10/29/pope-leo-xiv-mail-ballot-illinois-midterm-election" >voted absentee</a> despite having moved from the fair city more than 12 years ago.</p><p><i>James L. Vail, Dubuque, Iowa</i></p><h3>Keep exposing corruption </h3><p>Thanks for publishing Robert Herguth's informative <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/10/29/julie-roys-evangelical-christian-corruption-roys-report-web-site" >story</a> on Julie Roys' reporting on corruption in evangelical Christian congregations and organizations. Herguth and other "Watchdogs" reporters at the Sun-Times do a great job of sniffing out the most egregious conduct of the slimeballs who masquerade as pillars of the community. I hope you will continue to unmask these people.</p><p><i>Sherry Szilage Stoffel, North Aurora</i><br></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Workplace assault leaves lasting scars
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I was sexually assaulted at work about 20 years ago. I went through an off-and-on cycle with that supervisor for almost a year. He used many different tactics: isolating me, befriending me, apologizing insincerely, stating that he was a pillar of the community and no one would believe it, and even telling me I hadn't meant it when I said no. At the same time, my then-husband started drinking and also became abusive toward me.</p><p>I left the job a year later after another incident occurred and the company swept it under the rug. Here I am, more than 20 years later, still dealing with the aftermath of that time period. I moved to another state for 18 years and thought it was all behind me. I moved back to my hometown last year, and I fell apart all over again. The triggers were intense at times. As a result, my current husband and I are moving to another state.</p><p>I hate that my life and my kids' lives were destroyed, and once again, I am leaving. I can't fix anything or change the truth, and I have to live with the fallout every day! I had a good family before it all happened. I stood up to my boss for a long time until I got to the point where I just didn't care anymore. No one should ever have to go through something like that. I am going to get a special form of PTSD therapy after I move, but I will never be the same. If you have any ideas, please let me know. — <i>DAMAGED IN THE EAST</i></p><p><b>DEAR DAMAGED:</b> I agree that no one should ever have to go through that. Your story is an important reminder that workplace sexual assault is an ongoing problem. I'm glad you plan to get the help you need. Your therapist is much better equipped to help you at this point than I am.</p><p>Readers, if you are ever sexually assaulted in the workplace, secure as much evidence as you can and go straight to the police. Do not start the process by going to the higher-ups in the company or the human resources department. Every one of those people will prioritize protecting the company over seeking justice for you. Consult a lawyer specializing in sexual abuse who can advise you on when and how to make your report to HR.</p><p>RAINN (rainn.org) — the Rape, Abuse and Incest National Network — operates a national hotline at 1-800-656-4673. Please call them if you ever have any questions about sexual assault of any kind.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> We have a number of cats in our household, and my son-in-law lives downstairs with his wife. He knows we love cats, and he sends me "funny" pictures of cats via text message two or three times a day. How do I tell him to stop doing this without hurting his feelings? — <i>'FELINE' IT'S TOO MUCH</i></p><p><b>DEAR 'FELINE':</b> Because your son-in-law's messages interrupt your routine, ask him to please save them and send them en masse once a week at a time when you can enjoy them.</p><p>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127. </p>

entries.title: Planting the seeds of healing for church sex abuse survivors
entries.summary: <p>Twenty years ago, I was forced to reckon with a secret I’d kept for more than three decades. That morning, I opened the newspaper to see my abuser named in a civil lawsuit for sexually abusing young boys years before. </p><p>I recognized the names of the plaintiffs — my former classmates.</p><p>It was emotionally and physically triggering. For days, I couldn’t sleep. I was nauseous, anxiety-ridden, and I didn't want to introduce this depraved story into my marriage. But I knew it was time to finally share my secret with my wife and face whatever came next.</p><p>I was sexually abused by my priest when I was a child. He had groomed our North Shore community, earning — then betraying — the trust of the children he was entrusted to protect and the parents who believed he was providing their children with spiritual mentorship.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-630000" name="module-630000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>Today, I understand that the abuse imposed upon me as a child inflicted wounds that take a lifetime to heal. But healing is never linear, and it cannot happen alone.</p><p>My healing began when the people I trusted with my story met me with love, compassion and belief. My wife, my priest and officials of the Archdiocese of Chicago, where I began the Independent Review Board process. I came to understand that the abuse I endured is obviously a part of who I am, but it does not define me.</p><p>While painful to recall the traumatic memories, the process of reporting my abuse to the church was also deeply healing. To be believed was critical to my experience. It showed me that faith and the church could be an important part of my journey, and that seeking accountability did not require me to turn my back either.</p><p>In fact, by working alongside the church, I have seen that true accountability is achieved by listening to survivors, then working together to create change. Fifteen years ago, I helped spearhead the creation of the Archdiocese of Chicago's <a class="Link" href="https://agresponse.archchicago.org/documents/5724603/5724668/Healing+Garden+Brochure+-+EN/92781587-9d70-4fcc-95ee-f469fc583568" target="_blank" >Healing Garden</a>. This powerful collaboration between the church and survivors provides a place for healing, even for those who can no longer set foot in a church. It is a permanent and public reminder that survivors are believed, valued and welcomed in this space. Each year, our survivor community gathers in the garden before the Mass of Hope and Healing for abuse survivors and family members. This year’s Mass took place last month, marking its 15th anniversary.</p><p>Chicago’s Healing Garden has now inspired the creation of a new <a class="Link" href="https://www.catholic.edu/info-for-the-media/media-releases/national-healing-garden-planned-catholic-university-america" target="_blank" >National Healing Garden</a> on the campus of the Catholic University of America in Washington, D.C. I am humbled to lead that effort alongside fellow survivors of abuse, so our voices continue to be heard.</p><p>Like our garden in Chicago, the planned garden in D.C. will provide a safe place for individual reflection and prayer, as well as community programming that brings people together, helps rebuild trust in the church and institutions that have been fractured by abuse and start conversations that protect the dignity and safety of God’s children.</p><p>Efforts like these are only possible when there is good, productive communication between the church and survivors. And they are proof that when we come together, we can foster healing which, like the gardens, can take root and grow.</p><p>Many struggle to understand how I have remained steadfast in my faith, and why my wife and I chose to raise our children in the church after what happened to me. I understand the question. But when I watched my own children as altar servers, I did not feel fear.</p><p>I felt joy that they could have the powerful, dignified experience I was denied. And I felt gratitude knowing that because people like me and my fellow survivors came forward, breaking the silence that surrounds childhood abuse, we helped prevent abuse from happening to the next generation.</p><p>Twenty years ago, I could never have imagined how far that first decision to tell my story would take me. I have learned that institutional accountability and personal healing are not the same. In keeping with archdiocesan policies, my abuser’s name is public, an important acknowledgment of the evil he committed. But I am still a deeply wounded person.</p><p>My abuse will always be a part of me, and my healing will be a lifelong journey. But I have found comfort knowing that I have people willing to listen, leaders willing to work alongside me, and a profound sense of faith lighting the way.</p><p><i>Michael Hoffman is chair of the Archdiocese of Chicago's Hope and Healing Committee and executive director of National Catholic Restorative Justice Initiative. The Chicago resident previously served as a president of Prevent Child Abuse Illinois.</i> </p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-e50000" name="module-e50000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Review: City Lit's 'King Hedley II' puts August Wilson on a small stage, and audiences are better for it
entries.summary: <p>Seeing an August Wilson play on a small stage is always a unique experience. But the intimacy of City Lit Theatre, located on the second floor of an Edgewater church, makes the intensity of gritty drama “King Hedley II” feel especially immersive.</p><p>This production is directed by Manny Buckley, a City Lit artistic associate who recently mounted Wilson’s “Seven Guitars,” a play that includes some of the same characters and storylines as “King Hedley II.” (Buckley’s production won the 2024 Non-Equity Jeff Award for best production). This play transports the audience to a Reagan-era Pittsburgh and, in it, an underserved neighborhood enduring the harsh effects of trickle-down economics.</p><p>It’s 1985 in Pittsburgh’s Hill District, and King Hedley (James Lewis) has recently been released from prison for killing the man who left a grotesquely visible scar across his face. King is trying to build a new life. When the audience meets him, he’s bent over a patch of dirt planting seeds — a running parallel in the show will be the new life the ex-con attempts to cultivate in that dirt.</p><p>King lives with his mother, Ruby (Andrea Conway-Diaz), a former singer who didn’t raise him and instead left him in the care of a friend. His wife, Tanya (Isis Elizabeth), is pregnant. Along with his friend Mister (Ernest Henton), King sells stolen refrigerators in hopes of one day opening his own video store business.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div Bryn Mawr Ave.<br><b>When:</b> Through Nov. 29<br><b>Info: </b>Tickets from $38<br><br></div> </div><p>James Lewis delivers a masterclass in his embodiment of King. Perhaps the proximity of the audience to the stage in this production is a factor, but from my seat I could feel his rage. King is ambitious. Through all the adversity he’s faced, both self-imposed and some inherited, he still has a strong sense of self.</p><p>Blood-for-blood is a recurring phrase in the play and vengeance is prevalent, but underneath the visceral nature of violence and revenge, King has dignity — he commands respect. He’s willing to die for it.</p><p>As King, Lewis moves from ambition to desperation seamlessly. He ping-pongs from moments of begging Tanya not to have an abortion —- literally pleading for life — to moments where he demands death. It’s a tough role to play, and Lewis nails it.</p><p>This play builds on characters and stories from past Wilson plays, including “Seven Guitars” and “Gem of the Ocean." But in true Wilson fashion, the production stands alone. You don’t need the past context to understand what happens here.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" class="Figure-credit"><p>Steven Townshend</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Outside of the connections to his own work, it's also hard to miss the ways Black playwrights influence each other. <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts/2024/09/05/lorraine-hansberry-statue-alison-saar-navy-pier-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>Lorraine Hansberry’s</u></a> classic play “A Raisin in the Sun,” presents Walter Lee Younger, who wants to achieve financial security in the 50s by opening a liquor store. In Dominique Morrisseau's “<a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/theater-stages/2026/09/23/review-eta-creative-arts-foundation-detroit-67-dominique-morisseau" target="_blank" ><u>Detroit 67</u></a>,” recently staged on the South Side, Lank, who along with his sister inherits a home from their parents, sees the path to Black freedom through business ownership, and wants to open a bar in the 1960s. Here, in the 1980s, King wants to build a future that hinges on opening a video store.</p><p>The barriers to King achieving his ultimate dream are the elements that make this play so powerful. He never goes to a bank for a business loan — that’s so farfetched it isn't considered. He attempts to hustle way to freedom, but he’s hindered by years of generational trauma, systemic oppression and an underserved neighborhood plagued by aimless youth committing crimes, like robbing the community’s elders.</p><p>Passed-down trauma is inescapable here. Watching the show, it’s clear where fate is taking King, yet he fights like hell to control his own destiny. But when Ruby’s former lover Elmore (Jelani Julyus) returns, he unearths a secret that explodes into gunfire.</p><p>All of this action unfolds on a cozy set designed by Jeremiah Barr. Wilson is so deft with language that this three-hour production, all happening behind Ruby's house, never feels stale. Even though characters never leave the backyard, lighting designer Mike McShane transports the audience into a surreal world during monologues with his clever use of tones and textures that drive home the emotion of actors.</p><p>This play has always reminded me of the Tupac poem “The Rose that Grew from Concrete.” In that poem, a beautiful flower grows, against all odds, in an unlikely place. Here, we see King, hands in the dirt trying to cultivate life that will beat all odds. </p><p>At one point, Elmore steps on King's budding plant, sending him into a fury. That’s an excellent use of foreshadowing, and encapsulates the play. Sometimes, our fates are sealed long before we are born.</p>

entries.title: Maybe it will happen today, one Chicago pessimist hopes. Thousands of fans do too.
entries.summary: <p>It was March of 2025, and everything sucked. Finances had been tough for a few years for Chicago artist Phineas X. Jones, 53, and he was deeply troubled by the reelection of President Donald Trump. Even so, the times planted a seed for him. In spite of it all, Jones doodled some flowers and sunshine and happy little animals on his iPad, framing a monumental set of words: Maybe it will happen today.</p><p>“I’m kind of on the pessimistic side anyway, so ‘maybe it could happen today’ is as optimistic as I get,” he said. “It’s possible a good thing could happen. I won’t rule it out.”</p><p>He <a class="Link" href="https://bsky.app/profile/today-maybe.bsky.social" target="_blank" ><u>posted the image</u></a> on Bluesky, a social media platform for people who miss the old Twitter. Then he just kept drawing: the same phrase, in endlessly different contexts. Jones has rendered the words as a page from an <a class="Link" href="https://bsky.app/profile/today-maybe.bsky.social/post/3lndfotestk23" target="_blank" ><u>illuminated manuscript</u></a>, alongside <a class="Link" href="https://bsky.app/profile/today-maybe.bsky.social/post/3mdihgeqjf22g" target="_blank" ><u>Pinhead</u></a> from the “Hellraiser” series, as an unfinished <a class="Link" href="https://bsky.app/profile/today-maybe.bsky.social/post/3mwdtcwub3c24" target="_blank" ><u>“Wheel of Fortune” board</u></a>, in an <a class="Link" href="https://bsky.app/profile/today-maybe.bsky.social/post/3mrwzbubjyc2e" target="_blank" ><u>Federal Art Project-style woodcut</u></a>, in homage to <a class="Link" href="https://bsky.app/profile/today-maybe.bsky.social/post/3lqac37r7cc2n" target="_blank" ><u>René Magritte’s surrealism</u></a>. More than 200 variations on a theme later, Jones has amassed some 12,000 followers.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-f50000" name="image-f50000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/32c6d46/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcb%2F5c%2F7739ea634e9088fcc64b3af618db%2Fmaybeitwill-261102-002.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8a8b585/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcb%2F5c%2F7739ea634e9088fcc64b3af618db%2Fmaybeitwill-261102-002.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/da727ea/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcb%2F5c%2F7739ea634e9088fcc64b3af618db%2Fmaybeitwill-261102-002.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Artist Phineas X. Jones, a native of Fort Collins, Colorado, has lived in Chicago for nearly three decades. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/da727ea/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcb%2F5c%2F7739ea634e9088fcc64b3af618db%2Fmaybeitwill-261102-002.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/07c88f0/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcb%2F5c%2F7739ea634e9088fcc64b3af618db%2Fmaybeitwill-261102-002.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/da727ea/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcb%2F5c%2F7739ea634e9088fcc64b3af618db%2Fmaybeitwill-261102-002.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Artist Phineas X. Jones, a native of Fort Collins, Colorado, has lived in Chicago for nearly three decades. “I’m kind of on the pessimistic side anyway, so ‘maybe it could happen today’ is as optimistic as I get,” he says. “It’s possible a good thing could happen. I won’t rule it out.”</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>On Oct. 22, he <a class="Link" href="https://www.kickstarter.com/projects/miwht2027/maybe-it-will-happen-today-the-2027-calendar/description" target="_blank" ><u>launched a Kickstarter</u></a> offering a 2027 calendar, with stickers and prints as extra perks; the campaign — running through Thursday morning — was funded within hours and has raised more than five times its original goal.</p><p>Jones doesn’t self-promote, other than by staying consistent with his posting. His only focus as an artist, he says, is the vibe, a particular balance of hope with exasperation or frustration. “It” should never be specific, although fans of the drawings tend to respond as though it were. Furthermore, the process should not stress him out. Jones doesn’t plan his drawings or solicit requests. His standard is “it looks cool, and it was fun to draw.”</p><p>For such a hopeful conceit, Jones often returns to villains in the project. Sho’nuff from “The Last Dragon” <a class="Link" href="https://bsky.app/profile/today-maybe.bsky.social/post/3lxcm5soh722f" target="_blank" ><u>blazes with the words</u></a>, while Tim Curry’s towering red devil Darkness from “Legend” <a class="Link" href="https://bsky.app/profile/today-maybe.bsky.social/post/3lnxf3q2xxs27" target="_blank" ><u>cackles beside it</u></a>. Nosferatu (2024) <a class="Link" href="https://bsky.app/profile/today-maybe.bsky.social/post/3lndflzfpy223" target="_blank" ><u>looms beneath it</u></a>, and Sideshow Bob threatens Bart Simpson with — what else? — a <a class="Link" href="https://bsky.app/profile/today-maybe.bsky.social/post/3mq2o53y7tk2i" target="_blank" ><u>belly tattoo</u></a>. primed to love his work. For a decade, Jones illustrated labels for Half Acre Beer Co., and he’s also designed screen-printed posters for bands and other brands. Although he’s a native of Fort Collins, Colorado, Jones has connected deeply with Chicago for the better part of three decades. Some of his other art includes what he calls “hot dog monsters” with a genealogy hinting at the <a class="Link" href="https://www.inprnt.com/gallery/phineas/maurie-flaurie/" target="_blank" ><u>Superdawg statues</u></a> atop the famous Norwood Park stand. One of his most popular prints <a class="Link" href="https://bsky.app/profile/today-maybe.bsky.social/post/3lndftdx7r223" target="_blank" ><u>depicts pigeons</u></a> atop the sign at the Belmont Red-Brown-Purple lines train platform.</p><p>The breadth of Jones’ influences, spanning both <a class="Link" href="https://bsky.app/profile/today-maybe.bsky.social/post/3msxpfpuauc2u" target="_blank" ><u>ancient Egyptian papyrus</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://bsky.app/profile/today-maybe.bsky.social/post/3mcrtwqa4q22c" target="_blank" ><u>remixed “Nancy” comics</u></a>, is part of the project’s delight, in addition to his grasp of so many different mediums and styles. Jones demurs: “I wouldn’t claim to be a master of anything, but I like doing all kinds of different stuff,” he said. “I’m pretty good at copying, so I can pick up a style off of something or somebody else.”</p><p>Not a single pixel of “Maybe It Will Happen Today” or any of Jones’ other art comes from artificial intelligence, he says. The suggestion is offensive to him; he includes information on his source material in replies and alt texts on his posts. The vast majority of his images are hand-drawn in Procreate, digital illustration software for the iPad; any outliers are usually photomanipulations, also made by hand.</p><p>“[AI is] all stolen work,” Jones said. “It looks bad. It’s boring and same-y. Jones</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>This deliberately low-tech and defiantly human approach has won Jones and “Maybe It Will Happen Today” thousands of fans. He tries not to let it get to him. As an artist, the pleasure of the project is in the process. “I can do whatever I want to, and however it turns out, that’s what it is,” he said. “I can’t get in trouble for it. Nobody gets to say I did it wrong.”</p><p>Perhaps someday, Jones muses, the appeal will fade or he’ll start looking like a tryhard. But his art is small-D democratic — deliberately accessible and absolutely something anybody can try for themselves. If anything, Jones’ work suggests the good thing that happens today might be someone stepping away from a chatbot prompt and picking up some art supplies. Whatever someone’s “it” happens to be, you can never rule it out.</p>
